historical_timeline.summary: Married Emperor Franz Joseph I in Vienna.
A mysterious illness with cough, poor nutrition and exhaustion; winter on Madeira and months on Corfu.
Restrictive diets, frequent weighing, tight lacing and hours of daily exercise.
Gave up riding because of health problems.
Death of her son at Mayerling; mourning and deepening depression afterwards.
Restless travel and the Achilleion on Corfu; swelling, pains and sciatica in her last years.
Stabbed in Geneva by an anarchist; died the same day.

claims.statement: Elisabeth Amalie Eugenie, Duchess in Bavaria, called Sisi, was born on December 24, 1837, in Munich, the daughter of Duke Max in Bavaria and Duchess Ludovika.
She married her cousin, Emperor Franz Joseph I, on April 24, 1854, in the Augustinerkirche in Vienna, and became Empress of Austria and, later, Queen of Hungary. She had four children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context; no health fact about her husband or children is used in the modern episode.

source_links.locator: Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary

claims.statement: From about 1859 she was reported to suffer from a mysterious illness, with cough, poor nutrition, anemia and exhaustion; she spent the winter of 1860 to 1861 on Madeira and, after a relapse, four months on Corfu, and recovered quickly whenever she travelled.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Early documented ill health; no diagnosis is adopted.

source_links.locator: the mysterious illness from 1859; Madeira; Corfu
October 1860: nervous breakdowns, poor nutrition, anemia, exhaustion and cough

claims.statement: At 1.72 m she was unusually tall for a woman of her time, with an extremely slender figure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Gives her height; the modern height is set to it.

claims.statement: Through her life she followed many diets; for periods each meal was a single food, such as egg, a milk product, orange or broth, and her 'magic weight' was fifty kilos. In her last years she weighed herself up to three times a day, and in 1894 she weighed as little as 43.5 kg, a body mass index of about 14.7 at her height.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented restrictive eating and frequent weighing; the weights come from a biographical essay that relies on published biographies. Anchors the modern presenting problem.

source_links.locator: diets; fifty kilos; up to three times daily; 43.5 kg in 1894
maximal body weight only 50 kilograms; milk diet

claims.statement: Her waist measured only about 50 cm at its smallest, in tightly laced corsets and dresses sewn around it.

source_links.locator: a special corset; her waist was only 50 cm

claims.statement: She hiked for hours every day and had exercise rooms installed in her apartments; in the Vienna Hofburg the wall bars, high bar and rings are preserved, and she had a large gymnasium with heavy apparatus. She was one of the best horsewomen in Europe, but gave up riding at the beginning of the 1880s because of health problems.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented excessive exercise; anchors the modern compulsive exercise.

source_links.locator: hiked for hours every day; riding; gave up riding
wall bars, high bar and rings; large gymnasium

claims.statement: A psychiatrist's biographical essay writes that in her last years she was increasingly troubled by her undernutrition, with fluid accumulation in the body and severe bodily pains, and that she was diagnosed with chlorosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented swelling and pain in her last years; chlorosis is the period diagnosis and is not adopted.

source_links.locator: fluid accumulation, severe bodily pains, chlorosis

claims.statement: Eating-disorder researchers write that she sometimes suffered from edema as a consequence of severe starvation.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation of the swelling as hunger edema.

claims.statement: A Swiss newspaper reported in 2024 that letters kept by her spa physician at Bad Kissingen, found in the city archive, describe complaints including rheumatic attacks, sciatica, joint pain and hunger edema at the ankles.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Newspaper report of archival letters; the dates of most letters are not given. Supports the brief's sciatica and ankle swelling.

source_links.locator: Ischias- und Gelenkschmerzen; Hungerödeme an den Fussknöcheln

claims.statement: Psychiatrists and eating-disorder researchers have argued that she met the criteria for anorexia nervosa: one essay states that 'without doubt' she qualified, a German study describes fasting rituals, gymnastics, hours of riding, forced marches and a considerable fear of weight gain, and Hungarian researchers describe many features of anorexia nervosa and suggest it was closely related to depression.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective diagnosis; she was never so diagnosed. Anchors the modern eating disorder, which is synthetic.

claims.statement: On January 30, 1889, her son, Crown Prince Rudolf, born in 1858, was found dead with a young woman at the Mayerling hunting lodge; historians regard as certain only that he killed her and then himself.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded once, plainly, without method detail. The modern episode refers only to the death of her son as a bereavement.

source_links.locator: found dead at Mayerling on 30 January 1889; first killed Mary and then himself

claims.statement: It is said that her son's death prompted her to wear only mourning from then on. She suffered from ever-deepening depressions, which in her last years are thought to have developed into a kind of death-wish.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented grief and depression; anchors the modern depression and safety assessment. Not a modern diagnosis.

source_links.locator: wear only mourning; ever-deepening depressions; a kind of death-wish

claims.statement: After her son's death she sought to master her inner unrest with extended travels and a retreat to Corfu, where she had the Achilleion, a palatial villa, built; she lost interest in it once it was finished and left the island six years after its completion. She often travelled incognito.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places her in restless travel during the synthetic episode; her whereabouts in 1894 were not verified.

claims.statement: On September 10, 1898, in Geneva, she was stabbed by an Italian anarchist and died; she was buried in the Imperial Crypt (Kapuzinergruft) in Vienna on September 17, 1898.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognizing and managing a restrictive eating disorder in a 56-year-old woman who presents with weight loss, fatigue, ankle swelling and dizziness, with compulsive exercise and frequent self-weighing since early adulthood: DSM-5-TR anorexia nervosa, restricting type, in later life; medical stabilization under the APA 2023 guideline, the SAHM 2022 medical management paper (written for younger patients and applied with care), the AED medical care standards and the ASPEN refeeding consensus (orthostatic vital signs, ECG for bradycardia and QTc, electrolytes with phosphate and magnesium, glucose, thiamine before nutrition, refeeding risk, and admission thresholds); bone density by DXA; a multidisciplinary team with an eating disorders psychiatrist, a dietitian and CBT-E; recurrent depression with persistent grief, with a structured safety assessment and a safety plan; a gastroenteritis that threatens potassium and the QTc on sertraline; preventive care at 56; the privacy of a public figure; and continuity of care for a patient who travels for weeks at a time.

assessment_plan.display: Acute viral gastroenteritis with mild dehydration and hypokalemia
assessment_plan.assessment: A contact with the same illness, vomiting that has stopped and watery diarrhea without blood fit a viral gastroenteritis. She is mildly dehydrated with orthostatic hypotension, but drinking. Potassium 3.3 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, creatinine 0.78 mg/dL, glucose 72 mg/dL, magnesium 1.7 mg/dL. The ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 452 ms. In anorexia nervosa, low potassium and a low glucose reserve make this riskier than usual, and sertraline adds a little to QT risk, so ondansetron is not used; the vomiting has stopped and an antiemetic is not needed. Stool tests and antibiotics are not indicated for a short watery illness without blood or high fever under the IDSA guideline. Her account, the absence of knuckle calluses, parotid swelling and dental erosion, and the illness in her contact do not suggest purging

referral.question: Weight loss to a BMI of 16.0 with fatigue, ankle swelling, dizziness on standing and a slow pulse in a 56-year-old woman with restrictive eating, frequent self-weighing and hours of daily exercise since early adulthood, and recurrent depression with grief. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on the level of care and on restarting nutrition safely, and lead a multidisciplinary plan that she can follow while she travels and that protects her privacy
referral.pertinent_history: Weight 47.4 kg at 172 cm (BMI 16.0), about 6 kg lost over six months; for decades she has kept her weight below a fixed 50 kg, eaten single-food meals, laced tightly, weighed herself up to three times a day, walked four to six hours a day and done gymnastics each morning. Fatigue, cold intolerance, 1+ pitting edema of both ankles, and dizziness on standing. No vomiting, laxatives, diuretics or diet pills. Last menstrual period in her late forties. Seated blood pressure 96/62, pulse 52, temperature 36.0 C; lying 98/64 with pulse 50, standing after two minutes 86/58 with pulse 66. ECG: sinus bradycardia 52, QTc 438 ms, low voltage. Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 93 fL, white cells 3.4 x10^3/uL, platelets 168 x10^3/uL, sodium 136 and potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, glucose 68 mg/dL, magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, phosphate 3.0 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, ALT 52 U/L, TSH 2.2 mIU/L, CRP 1.0 mg/L, tissue transglutaminase IgA negative, ferritin 64 ng/mL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL. PHQ-9 16 with passive thoughts of death and no intent or plan; a safety plan is in place. Her son died five years ago and she has worn mourning since. Started today: thiamine 100 mg daily, vitamin D, and a meal plan of about 1,600 kcal a day. She travels for weeks at a time and is a public figure who fears exposure
questions: Is this anorexia nervosa, another specified feeding or eating disorder, or a medical illness, in a woman of 56 whose restriction began in early adulthood?
Can she be treated as an outpatient, and what findings should lead to admission?
How should nutrition be advanced, given her refeeding risk, and how should she be monitored?
What psychological treatment and team do you recommend, given her travel and her need for privacy?
How should her depression, grief and passive thoughts of death be treated alongside the eating disorder, and when should an antidepressant start?
What should be done about her exercise and her bones?

consultant_note.history: Empress Elisabeth, 56, is seen at the request of Dr. Marchetti-Osei. Since her late teens she has restricted her eating, with single-food meals, a fixed upper weight of 50 kg that she has kept below for decades, tight lacing, and four to six hours of fast walking a day with gymnastics each morning; she feels anxious and guilty if she cannot exercise. She weighs herself up to three times a day. Over six months she has lost about 6 kg, and she has become tired, cold, dizzy on standing and swollen at the ankles. She describes an intense fear of gaining weight and sees herself as larger than she is, though she accepts that she is too thin. She denies binge eating, vomiting, laxatives, diuretics or diet pills. Her mood has been low for years, worse since the death of her son five years ago, a bereavement by suicide; she has passive thoughts of being better off dead without intent, plan or past attempts. She has had a week of the meal plan and thiamine, missed the blood test planned for three to four days, and has walked about two hours a day. She travels constantly and fears that her illness will become public
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Marchetti-Osei's intake note, ECG and tests (sinus bradycardia 52, QTc 438 ms; hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white cells 3.4 x10^3/uL, glucose 68 mg/dL, ALT 52 U/L, TSH 2.2 mIU/L, CRP 1.0 mg/L, tissue transglutaminase IgA negative, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL). Today, seven days into the meal plan: sodium 137, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, phosphate 2.3 mg/dL, magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, glucose 74 mg/dL. Weight 47.9 kg, BMI 16.2

exam.finding: Very thin, tall woman; weight 47.9 kg; temperature 36.1 C
Lying blood pressure 100/64, pulse 52; standing 90/60, pulse 68; 1+ ankle edema
Dry skin; fine lanugo-like hair on the forearms; no calluses on the knuckles; no parotid swelling
Articulate, guarded, courteous; mood low, affect constricted; preoccupied with weight and shape; passive thoughts of death without intent or plan; no psychotic features; insight partial

assessment.assessment: Restriction leading to a significantly low weight, intense fear of weight gain with persistent behavior that prevents it, and a disturbed experience of her body meet the DSM-5-TR criteria for anorexia nervosa; with no binge eating or purging in the last three months it is the restricting type, and a BMI of 16.0 at intake is moderate. OSFED does not apply because all criteria are met. Most anorexia nervosa in later life, as here, began in youth and became long-standing. The normal TSH, CRP, celiac antibody and electrolytes, with low rather than high glucose, make thyroid disease, inflammation, celiac disease, diabetes and adrenal insufficiency unlikely; no further tests are needed. Compulsive exercise is part of the disorder

She does not meet the thresholds for admission: her pulse is above 40 awake, systolic pressure above 90, temperature above 35.6 C, potassium above 3.0 mmol/L, and she is eating. Admission would be advised for any of those, for fainting, chest pain or arrhythmia, phosphate below 2.0 mg/dL, a fall in weight despite treatment, or food refusal. Her phosphate of 2.3 mg/dL is an early refeeding effect that needs replacement and weekly checks. The slightly worse ankle edema is refeeding edema; a diuretic would worsen it later

A recurrent moderate depressive episode with persistent grief, bereavement by suicide, and passive thoughts of death without intent or plan. Antidepressants work poorly at very low weight and starvation mimics depression, so nutrition comes first; an SSRI with low QT risk, such as sertraline, is reasonable once nutrition is under way and the ECG is repeated

Decades of low weight and her age put her at high risk of low bone mass; DXA is indicated. Weight restoration is the main treatment. Exercise should be limited while her pulse and blood pressure are abnormal

recommendations: Outpatient treatment: weekly weights at therapy, weekly blood tests for three weeks, and medical review by Dr. Marchetti-Osei in three weeks and at least every two months while underweight; admission for any of the thresholds above
Phosphorus 250 mg twice daily for three weeks; finish 14 days of thiamine; electrolytes, phosphate and magnesium weekly for three weeks, then at each visit while underweight
The dietitian to advance the meal plan by about 200 to 300 kcal every few days toward weight gain of 0.5 to 1 kg a week, with three meals and two to three snacks

Weekly enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E) with open weighing in the session, and an end to weighing at home; video sessions when she travels; psychiatry review by video at about four weeks and then as needed
No gymnastics and walks of no more than an hour a day for now, with a graded return agreed by the team once vital signs are normal and weight is rising

Sertraline 25 mg, then 50 mg, at about four weeks if the ECG is normal, with grief-focused work in therapy; safety review at every visit and the safety plan kept current, including crisis numbers abroad
DXA of the spine and hip at about four weeks, with calcium to about 1,200 mg a day and vitamin D
Privacy: a restricted chart, a scheduling alias, and secure video; information shared only with her consent
